questions.q: At a weekly haat in Hyderabad, Gopal buys turmeric powder in three sacks of 2450 g each and one sack of 500 g. questions.a: (a) 8. (b) 22 pieces with 0.4 m left. (c) Dupattas ₹5120; blouse pieces ₹5280. (d) Blouse pieces earn ₹160 more but leave 0.4 m unusable, while dupattas use all 18 m. Either choice is acceptable if the reasons use these figures; blouse pieces give more money.

questions.q: A shopkeeper says a 12 m ribbon cut into pieces of 0.4 m gives 3 pieces. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: 3 pieces of 0.4 m make only 1.2 m, not 12 m. 12 ÷ 0.4 = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 pieces.
s: Notes 1.2 m is far less than 12 m

questions.q: Which of these divisions does NOT give 49?
A school bus covers 187.5 km in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.a: 75 km per hour

questions.q: A school bus carrying students to Mahabaleshwar covers 187.5 km in 2 h 30 min on the first stretch and 135 km in 2 h 15 min on the second. For the last 105 km the driver can take the hill road at 52.5 km per hour, or the highway at the first-stretch speed with a toll of ₹180 that the school has not budgeted. The lunch venue is booked at 2.1 hours from now. (a) Find the speed on the first stretch. (b) Find the speed on the second stretch. (c) How long does the hill road take for 105 km? (d) Both roads reach the venue in time. Which one would you choose? Give a reason with figures.
questions.a: (a) 2 h 30 min = 2.5 h, so 75 km/h. (b) 2 h 15 min = 2.25 h, so 60 km/h. (c) 2 hours. (d) Highway: 105 ÷ 75 = 1.4 hours, arriving 0.6 hour earlier but with ₹180 extra. Hill road: 2 hours, within 2.1, no toll, but only 0.1 hour to spare. Either choice is acceptable with a reason: the highway buys a safety margin of 0.7 hours, the hill road saves ₹180.
s: Part (a): converts 2 h 30 min to 2.5 h and divides to get 75 km/h
Part (b): converts 2 h 15 min to 2.25 h and divides to get 60 km/h
Part (d): compares time margin (0.7 h against 0.1 h) with the ₹180 toll and gives a reasoned choice

questions.q: Write a division of a counting number by a decimal whose quotient is 40, and check it by multiplication.
questions.a: For example 20 ÷ 0.5 = 200 ÷ 5 = 40. Check: 40 × 0.5 = 20, which is the original 20.
s: Division stated, with a decimal divisor
Check by multiplying quotient and divisor

questions.a: (a) 525 ÷ 35. (b) 15, which is more than 5.25 because the divisor 0.35 is between 0 and 1.
s: Part (b): 15, greater than 5.25 since the divisor is below 1

questions.q:
Match each division in Column I with its quotient in Column II, using 648 ÷ 24 = 27.

Tanvi says, "Dividing always gives a smaller number than we began with." Is she right? Test with 96 ÷ 4 and 96 ÷ 0.4 and say when she is right.
questions.a: No. 96 ÷ 4 = 24 is smaller, but 96 ÷ 0.4 = 240 is bigger. She is right only when the divisor is greater than 1.

questions.q: Rewrite 9 3/4 ÷ 1 1/2 using decimals. (a) Write both numbers as decimals. (b) Divide.

questions.a: (a) 0.1666… (b) Each remainder is 4, so the digit 6 repeats and the division never ends.
s: Part (b): remainder 4 repeats after the first digit

questions.q: Why can the long division of 1 by 7 never give more than 6 different non-zero remainders?
questions.a: Every remainder is less than 7, so it is one of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. A zero remainder ends the division, so only 1 to 6 are possible.
s: Remainder is less than the divisor 7
Zero ends the division, leaving 6 non-zero values

questions.a: 3 only

questions.q: Compare 1 ÷ 7, 10 ÷ 3 and 3 ÷ 5. For each say whether it ends, how many different non-zero remainders occur, and why.
questions.a: 1 ÷ 7: never ends; remainders 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5 (six) then repeat. 10 ÷ 3: never ends; the one remainder 1 repeats. 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6: ends, as the remainder reaches 0. In each case the remainders are fewer than the divisor, so either the division ends or a remainder repeats.
s: States the general reason: fewer remainders than the divisor

questions.a: Each remainder is one of 1 to 6 (zero would end the division). After 6 steps all six values could be used up, so the 7th remainder must be one already seen, and then the digits repeat.
s: States remainders can only be 1 to 6
Concludes a remainder repeats, so digits cycle

questions.q: The maths club of a Bhopal school studies 3 ÷ 7 by long division. For its poster it wants a repeating block of at most three digits with at least two different digits, and it is choosing between 1 ÷ 11 and 1 ÷ 37. (a) Write the first six digits of 3 ÷ 7 after the decimal point. (b) List the remainders after each of those digits. (c) Which digit is the 20th after the decimal point in 3 ÷ 7? (d) Find the repeating block of 1 ÷ 11 and of 1 ÷ 37 and say which you would put on the poster, giving one advantage of each.
questions.a: (a) 0.428571… (b) 2, 6, 4, 5, 1, 3. (c) The block 428571 has length 6 and 20 = 3 × 6 + 2, so the 20th digit is the 2nd digit of the block: 2. (d) 1 ÷ 11 = 0.0909… (block 09, 2 digits, remainders 1 and 10 only); 1 ÷ 37 = 0.027027… (block 027, 3 digits, remainders 1, 10, 26). Both fit. 1 ÷ 11 is quicker to check by hand; 1 ÷ 37 shows three different digits and fills the poster better. Either choice with such a reason is accepted. (3 ÷ 7 itself has a six-digit block and does not fit.)
s: Part (c): finds the 20th digit as 2 using the block length 6
Part (d): finds blocks 09 and 027 and gives a reasoned choice with an advantage of each

A division by 6 that never ends, with quotient 0.1666…

questions.q: Divide 2 by 7 by long division. Write the first eight digits after the decimal point, list the remainders after each digit, and say where the remainders start repeating.
questions.a: 2 ÷ 7 = 0.28571428… The remainders after each digit are 6, 4, 5, 1, 3, 2, 6, 4. Starting remainder 2 returns after 6 digits, so the digits 285714 repeat.
s: Notes the remainder 2 returns after 6 steps

questions.q: The book-fair stall committee of a Chennai school has ₹100 of prize money to share equally among its volunteers, and money can only be paid in rupees and paise. The stall cannot run with fewer than 10 volunteers. One choice is a team of 8 volunteers who are all experienced; the other is a team of 11. (a) Write the share of one volunteer as a decimal if 11 volunteers share it, up to four digits after the point. (b) If each of the 11 is paid ₹9.09, what is the total paid and how much is left? (c) If only 8 volunteers share it, what is each share? (d) Which team would you recommend? Use the staffing rule and the paisa left over in your reasons.
questions.a: (a) ₹9.0909… (b) 11 × 9.09 = ₹99.99, so ₹0.01 is left. (c) ₹12.5 = ₹12.50. (d) The team of 8 pays exactly but breaks the rule of at least 10 volunteers. The team of 11 meets the rule and the ₹0.01 can go to one volunteer (₹9.10) or to the class fund. Recommend the team of 11, or the team of 8 only if extra unpaid helpers make up the numbers. A reasoned choice is accepted.
s: Part (d): weighs exact payment against the staffing rule and handles the left-over paisa

questions.q: A diary press prints one page for every day from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2027. How many pages does it print?
Ritu says, "2400 is a leap year, because it is a century year and it is divisible by 400." Do you agree? Explain with the rule, and say what would happen to 2300.
questions.a: Yes. 2400 ÷ 400 = 6, so the century-year rule is met and 2400 is a leap year. 2300 ÷ 400 is 5.75, so 2300 is not a leap year even though it is divisible by 4.
s: Notes 2300 is not divisible by 400 so it is not leap

questions.q: A press in Sivakasi prints a planner with one page for every day from 1 January 2096 to 31 December 2104, both included. Paper comes in packs of 500 sheets at ₹1150 a pack, or in reams of 1000 sheets at ₹2150 a ream, and one sheet makes one page. (a) How many pages are needed for 2096 to 2099? (b) How many pages are needed for 2100 to 2104? (c) Find the total number of pages. (d) Which order of reams and packs gives at least that many sheets at the lowest cost? Show the cost of two other orders you compared.
questions.a: (a) 4 × 365 + 1 = 1461. (b) 5 × 365 + 1 = 1826 (only 2104 is a leap year, 2100 is not). (c) 1461 + 1826 = 3287. (d) 3 reams and 1 pack = 3500 sheets for ₹7600, the cheapest. 7 packs = 3500 sheets for ₹8050; 4 reams = 4000 sheets for ₹8600; 3 reams alone give only 3000 sheets and fall short.
s: Part (b): 1826 pages, excluding the leap day in 2100
Part (d): finds 3 reams + 1 pack at ₹7600 by comparing with 7 packs at ₹8050 and 4 reams at ₹8600

questions.q: (a) How many years in 100 calendar years are divisible by 4, and how many of them stay leap years if century years are excluded? (b) Find the total days.
questions.a: (a) 25 years are divisible by 4; excluding the 100th year leaves 24. (b) 24 × 366 + 76 × 365 = 36524.

questions.a: (a) 100. (b) 100 - 4 + 1 = 97. (c) Rule A: 146100; Rule B: 146097. (d) Earth: 146096.88. Rule A is longer by 3.12 days; Rule B by 0.12 days. Rule B is much closer, so prefer B.
s: Part (d): differences 3.12 and 0.12 days, prefers Rule B
